docs.title: Infinity Base Comparison
docs.text:
Season 14 · Act 2 Desert Mercenary · Jab

Which ethereal 4-socket polearm or spear to put Infinity in, for an Act 2 mercenary that attacks with Jab. Every base is run at every item IAS from 0 to 150%: weapon damage per second, Crushing Blows per second, the time it takes to kill a target, and what the merc does while you teleport past monsters.

Reset to the defaultsCopy a link to this setup

Your mercenary Item IAS i % Merc level Infinity's damage roll +290% Superior base i None + Skills on merc gear Other damage i % Skill IAS i % Attacks i Jab 80%, basic 20% Jab only Crushing Blow chance i % Crushing Blow efficiency i % Critical Strike and Deadly Strike, from the merc's gear Critical Strike chance i 0% Critical Strike multiplier i % Deadly Strike chance i 0% Deadly Strike multiplier i % Maximum Deadly Strike i %

Target, for the kill time Target Map monster, example: 30,000 life Map boss, example: 300,000 life, 20% physical resistance Baal in Hell, 1 player: about 493,700 life, 50% physical resistance Custom Life Physical resistance % Each Crushing Blow takes 1/8 of current life (most monsters) 1/30 of current life (map bosses) 1/(70 + 10 × % of life missing) (prime evils) Nothing (kill time without Crushing Blow) Monster you teleport past Life i Physical resistance % Merc starts its attack i 2 frames after you land 3 frames after 4 frames after 5 frames after 6 frames after

Most damage per second

—

Most Crushing Blows

—

Fastest kill

—

Weapon damage per second

Average physical damage per second over the merc's Jabs and basic attacks, Critical and Deadly Strikes included, before the target's resistance. Higher is better. Each line is one speed group of elite bases; hover or tap for every group's value, click to set your IAS.

Crushing Blows per second

Every hit rolls Crushing Blow, both hits of a Jab included, so this follows the hit rate alone: the weapon's damage doesn't matter. Infinity's Chain Lightning (25% on striking) fires at the same rate, scaled to 25%.

Seconds to kill the target

Weapon damage (Critical and Deadly Strikes included) and Crushing Blow together, the merc alone. Lower is better. The more each hit does, the more the harder-hitting bases gain on the faster ones, whose edge is the extra Crushing Blows.

Teleporting past a monster

You land on a monster and teleport on one cast later: 8 frames at 105% FCR, 7 frames at 200% FCR. Your merc is moved to where you land in the same frame; if it's free, it acts 2 frames later and Jabs the monster beside it. That Jab plays out in full, both hits on that monster, even after your next teleport has moved the merc on with you: the hit never checks distance. The chart adds up what that one attack does to the monster set above, frame by frame from the frame you land, at your IAS; the markers show when you teleport on.

Base Speed Jab hits on frame Jab length The merc's attack on that monster Landings the merc attacks on, chain teleporting Damage Monster dead 200% FCR (7 frames) 105% FCR (8 frames)

Frames count from the frame you land (frame 0). The attack is one Jab (both hits) or, 20% of the time, one basic attack; damage is its average and "Monster dead" the share of 8,000 simulated attacks per base that kill the monster, with every damage roll, Crushing Blow, Critical Strike, and Deadly Strike rolled. A monster killed after you've moved on dies where you left it. While you chain teleport, the merc starts its next attack 2 frames after the last one's length, on whatever is beside it then, so it can attack on only as many landings as its attacks fit: hops of 7 or 8 frames against the length of a Jab (or of a basic attack). Bases of one speed group hit on the same frames; their kill chances differ only through their damage spread.

Every base at 40% IAS Exceptional and normal bases

Ethereal, with your Infinity roll and superior bonus. Ethereal lowers the Strength and Dexterity needed by 10. The best value of each column has a diamond. Within a speed group, average damage differs by about 1% at most, so pick by what your merc can wear. Amazon spears also take Infinity, but the merc can't wear them.

Base Speed Two-hand damage Str / Dex needed Merc level needed Jab length Damage / s Hits / s Crushing Blows / s Kill time

Exceptional and normal bases share the elite bases' speed groups with far less damage: none of them beats the elite base of its speed group.

Jab breakpoints

Item IAS needed for each Jab length, with your skill IAS. A Jab's length covers both of its hits; the merc starts its next attack 2 frames after it; 25 frames make one second.

Basic attack breakpoints

One hit per swing; the merc swings instead of Jabbing 20% of the time.

How it's worked out
  • Attack speed. Item IAS counts as ⌊120 × IAS / (120 + IAS)⌋. Add skill IAS, subtract the base's speed (negative is faster), cap at 75: that's the total. The animation then advances ⌊256 × (100 + total) / 100⌋ per frame. The merc's Jab is a 14-step sequence with two hits (on steps 6 and 10), lasting ⌈256 × 14 / rate⌉ frames; its basic attack is a 16-frame swing with one hit (on frame 11), lasting ⌈256 × 16 / rate⌉ − 1. These give the PD2 wiki's Desert Guard breakpoints exactly. The merc starts its next attack 2 frames after either length: the game ends the attack a frame later, and the merc picks its next one the frame after that. So from one Jab to the next takes the IAS Calculator's frame count for the Desert Mercenary.
  • Attack mix. The merc uses Jab 80% of the time and a basic attack otherwise, so damage and hits per second are averages over that mix (or Jab alone, if you pick it).
  • Damage per hit. First the weapon's own damage: the base's damage, times 1.25 for ethereal, raised by the weapon's enhanced damage, which is Infinity's roll plus a superior base's 5–20% (both are on the weapon, so they add up). That is the damage the weapon shows. A hit does the weapon's damage times (100 + the Strength and Dexterity bonus + Jab's bonus + other damage %) / 100: enhanced damage on the merc's other gear adds to those bonuses, not to the weapon's. Polearms and spears give 0.75% per point of Strength and of Dexterity. Jab gives +30% at level 1 and +15% per level; the merc's Jab is level 24 from merc level 75 on, plus your + skills. A basic attack gets no Jab bonus. A Hell merc has 173 Strength and 139 Dexterity at level 75, then 1.75 and 1.5 more per level.
  • Critical Strike and Deadly Strike. Every hit, both Jab hits included, first rolls Critical Strike (at most 75%): it does 200% damage, plus any Critical Strike Multiplier. A hit that isn't a Critical Strike rolls Deadly Strike (at most 75%, plus any Maximum Deadly Strike): 150% damage, plus any Deadly Strike Multiplier, which adds to the 150% (Wraithskin's +25% makes it 175%). So 50% Deadly Strike alone makes the average hit 25% stronger, and 37.5% with Wraithskin. Only the hit's physical damage is raised; Crushing Blow takes the same share as without. Every base gains the same share, so neither changes which base does the most damage per second.
  • Crushing Blow. Every hit rolls the chance, both Jab hits included. A proc takes the target's current life divided by 8 for most monsters (normal, champion, unique, minion), 30 for map bosses, or 70 + 10 × the % of life it's missing for prime evils. A merc's Crushing Blow works exactly like a player's. Efficiency divides the divisor by (1 + efficiency), a missile multiplies it by 1.5, physical resistance lowers the damage (none at 100%), and with more players in the game the divisor grows (with one player it doesn't).
  • Kill time. Each hit removes the average damage (Critical and Deadly Strikes averaged in) and the average Crushing Blow (chance × share × life left), until no life is left; the hit count divided by hits per second is the time. The merc alone, one player. Baal's life and physical resistance are his Hell values with one player (6,336 base life at 7,792% for his level 99); the map monster and map boss are round examples, so type your own target's.
  • Teleporting. The sorceress's cast is 14 frames at the same speed scale. FCR counts as ⌊120 × FCR / (120 + FCR)⌋, at most 75, and a cast lasts ⌈256 × 14 / rate⌉ − 1 frames: 8 at 105% FCR, 7 at 200%. You land on one cast's teleport frame and leave on the next one's, so you stand on the monster for exactly one cast.
  • The merc during a pass. When you teleport, your merc is moved to where you land in the same frame (except in guild games). If it was free, it acts 2 frames later; if it was in the middle of an attack, that attack keeps going and keeps its target. A Jab's hits land ⌈256 × 5 / rate⌉ and ⌈256 × 9 / rate⌉ frames after it starts, a basic attack's at ⌈256 × 11 / rate⌉, and nothing checks distance between the hit frame and the damage, so a Jab finishes on its first target wherever the merc has been moved. When you walk or run away instead, the merc heads back once you're 19 subtiles away and it has no target (about 34 while it fights), and warps beside you past 48.
  • Not counted. Walking to a target, misses, Chain Lightning's damage, and the merc's own base damage.
Best at 40% IAS Damage / s Crushing Blows / s Kill time

docs.title: Item Builder
docs.text:
Season 14 · Gear · Affix odds

Pick a base, its quality, and how it's made, then the affixes you want: see how likely the item is, which item level or character level gives it best, the class skills and automagic it can roll, and how Erazure shows it.

Inspired by hiimpd2's Item Builder.

Loading the item tables…

The Item Builder runs in your browser: please turn JavaScript on.

How the chance is worked out
  • Affix level. The item level, raised to the base's quality level. A base with a magic level (circlets) adds it; any other base loses half its quality level, or near the top of the range gets twice the item level minus 99. Kept between 1 and 99.
  • What can roll. Every affix whose level is at or below the affix level (and its top level at or above), made for the item's type, and allowed on its quality: some only on magic items, some only on rares, and some not on crafts. An affix of a kind already on the item (two resist-all, two sockets) doesn't roll again.
  • How likely each is. Picked by weight among what can still roll. On an item that drops in a map, the Season 14 map affixes weigh more: tier 1 +20%, tier 2 +30%, tier 3 +40%, and tier 4 +50%, but no more than the map allows: 20% in T1 maps, 30% in T2, 40% in T3, and 50% in T4 dungeons. Nothing made in the cube gets this.
  • Magic items. A prefix only 1 time in 4, both 1 in 4, and a suffix only 1 in 2. Always both on charms from item level 90, rings, amulets, and jewels from 85, and anything else from 65.
  • Rare items. 6 affixes from item level 85; 5 or 6 from 65; 4 to 6 from 45; 3 to 6 below; jewels 4. Each is a prefix or a suffix, half and half, at most 3 of each.
  • Crafted items. The craft's fixed mods, plus 1 to 4 affixes: 4 from item level 71; below that, the item level sets the fewest (2 from 31, 3 from 51) and the rest is a roll. The cube makes the item at half your character level plus half the item level of the base you put in, each rounded down.
  • Rerolls. 3 Perfect Skulls make a new rare at 40% of your level plus 40% of the item's item level, each rounded down; 3 perfect gems make a new magic item at the item's own item level. A reroll is never ethereal.
  • Class skills. Class items (not Amazon items or Paladin shields, whose skills are automagic) roll none 1 time in 10, one skill 4 in 10, two 3 in 10, and three 2 in 10. Each is one of the class's skills, all as likely, but a skill needs an item level of its required level + 7. Each is +3 a quarter of the time, +2 35%, and +1 40% (from item level 30; lower item levels roll fewer +3s).
  • Automagic. Some bases always roll one extra mod from their own list (orbs' life or mana, staves' faster cast rate, and Amazon weapons' skill tabs), unless an affix of the same kind is on the item.
  • Level requirement. The highest level any of the item's prefixes and suffixes need, its automagic (not on crafts), its class skills, and the base's own. Crafting adds nothing on top. Some affixes need less for characters of one class.
  • Ethereal. 1 in 20 dropped weapons and armor that can be ethereal are.
  • The chance is worked out exactly from these rules, not drawn at random.

docs.title: LLD Item Guide
docs.text:
Season 14 · Gear · Low level dueling

Plan a low level dueling item for level 30, 18, or 9: every way to make it, ranked, and the item level to aim for.

How to use this guide
  1. Pick your bracket and class in Your bracket: level 30, 18, or 9. Some affixes need a lower level for one class.
  2. Say what you want: start from an item Erazure tags LLD, or pick a base and the affixes you want (type a stat, like resist or life). If you'll corrupt it, tick the corruptions you'd like under Then corrupt it.
  3. Read the ways to make it, likeliest first: each row is a way, with its chance per item (rare rings found, crafts, rerolls) and the item level it's at. The box under them says the item level to aim for and how to get there: where monsters of that level are, or the character level and item to craft with.
  4. Use the chart to see where each affix can roll and the chance at every item level: ★ marks the best, ◇ what's about as good. Click, tap, or use the arrow keys to pick another item level; the box follows. You choose the item level (where it drops, or what you craft with); its affix level follows from it. How the game works is under the guide.

On a phone the answer is at the top; what it's for is under it.

Loading the item tables…

The LLD Item Guide runs in your browser: please turn JavaScript on.

How it works item level, affixes, and the ways to make an item From item level to the level it needs
  1. Its item level. An item's item level is the same as the monster level of the monster that dropped it. A crafted item's item level comes from your character level and the item level of the item you put in, each part rounded down: Crafted item level = your character level ÷ 2 + the item's item level ÷ 2 For example, a level 30 character crafting with an item of item level 72 makes crafted item level 15 + 36 = 51. Rerolling a rare item with 3 Perfect Skulls gives the new rare 40% of each instead (so at most 78). Rerolling a magic item with 3 perfect gems keeps its item level.
  2. How many affixes it rolls. Item levelRareCrafted 1-303-61-4 31-443-62-4 45-504-62-4 51-644-63-4 65-705-63-4 71-845-64 85-9964 A rare's counts are each as likely. A craft's affixes come besides its fixed mods, and its lowest count is the likeliest: 1 affix 40% of the time up to item level 30, 2 affixes 60% at 31-50, and 3 affixes 80% at 51-70. A magic item has 1 or 2 (both a quarter of the time), always 2 from item level 65 (85 on rings, amulets, and jewels, 90 on charms).
  3. Its affix level. The item level minus half the base's quality level, rounded down, catching up near item level 99: the same as the item level on a Ring or an Amulet, 1 lower on Leather Gloves, and 14 lower on a Small Charm up to item level 85, then catching up: 81 at 90, 99 at 99.
  4. Which affixes can roll. Each affix only between its own lowest and highest affix level. The higher the affix level, the stronger the affixes that can roll and the more of them need more than your bracket, while the weakest stop at their highest.
  5. The level it needs. The highest of: the base itself (a Diadem needs 64, so it can never be an LLD item), each of its prefixes and suffixes, on magic and rare items its automagic (an orb's life, a Paladin shield's resistances, or an Amazon weapon's skill tab: the stronger ones need more than 30), each class skill on it, and whatever is socketed in it. Some affixes need less for characters of one class (the charge suffixes), so pick your class above.
The ways to make an item Drops

A dropped item's item level is the monster level of the monster that dropped it: champions are 2 levels above their area's monsters, unique monsters 3.

The lower the item level, the fewer strong affixes can roll, and the fewer of them need more than your bracket.

The kills count every monster you'd kill clearing the area, its champions and unique monsters as often as they spawn, for one player, with the magic find you enter (a map adds its own). Magic find raises the chance of a rare, not of a magic ring, amulet, charm, or jewel. A party of three or more near you makes ordinary monsters drop about 10% more.

Crafting

A magic or rare item of the craft's type, with the recipe's ingredients or its craft infusion, becomes a crafted item of the same base: the craft's fixed mods plus 1 to 4 affixes of its own. Its old affixes don't carry over, but an ethereal item makes an ethereal craft. Crafted item levels go up to 98.

Crafting adds nothing to the level it needs, and neither do the fixed mods (Diablo II added 10, plus 3 per affix; Project Diablo 2 doesn't).

Rerolling a magic item with 3 perfect gems

Used mostly on magic Small Charms and Grand Charms. It rerolls the item's affixes and keeps its base and item level, so each try is as likely to give what you want as a drop of that item level. You can reroll as often as you have gems.

Buying from a vendor

In Normal difficulty a store's items have your character level + 5 as their item level, at most 12, 20, 28, 36, and 45 in Acts 1 to 5, so a character of any level higher shops at that act's most. A vendor sells magic copies of a base only from an item level of its own, and non-magical ones below 25.

Stores sell magic armor and weapons (claws, daggers, scepters, wands, and staves among them, and quivers), but no rings, amulets, jewels, charms, circlets, orbs, Amazon weapons, or class helms and shields. Nightmare and Hell stores sell upgraded bases instead, so the guide counts Normal's.

Rerolling a rare item with 3 Perfect Skulls

Used mostly on rare jewels. A new rare of the same base, at 40% of your character level plus 40% of the item's item level, each rounded down (so at most 78). It is never ethereal.

Each try costs 3 Perfect Skulls, so it rarely pays for LLD gear.

Bricking with a Worldstone Shard

Corrupting an item with no sockets can turn it into a rare of the same base and item level: half the time for a non-magical weapon, armor, or quiver, and a quarter of the time for a magic item, rings and amulets included. Each try costs a shard and the item.

The rare comes corrupted, with a corruption of its own: one of a rare's corruptions other than turning into another rare, each a third likelier than when you corrupt one. Erazure's LLD tags count a point for an uncorrupted item, so a bricked one needs one point more, or a corruption that gives it.

docs.title: Map Event and Boss Rushing
docs.text:
Season 14 · Maps · Map events

A character that teleports can run rare T1–T3 maps without clearing them (scout the map for its map event, do the event, kill the map boss, and open the next map): this page compares those runs with full clears, an hour of each, at your own times; and when you get a unique map, rush its bosses.

  1. Open a rare map rolled the way you like it. Rolling for low monster density only buys a safer scout: the events and the boss don't depend on it.
  2. Teleport over the whole map. Map events spawn as the rooms around you fill with monsters, not as monsters die, so a scout finds an event as surely as a full clear does.
  3. Do the event when its message shows, unless you skip it. The Dark Wanderer, the Treasure Fallen, and the Corrupted Heroes always bring all three, so stop scouting after the third.
  4. Kill the map boss, which you'll have passed on the scout, and open the next map.
  • When events show: the Spire of Darkness within the first few teleports; the Dark Wanderer, the Treasure Fallen, and the Corrupted Heroes from about a quarter of the way in; the Bitter Depths, Horazon, the Shadow of Mendeln, Gheed, and the Altar of the Catalyst about halfway through the scout.
  • What decides it: your time a map besides the scout (making the game, opening the map, and town) and how long your full clears take. The calculator below shows where the runs pull ahead at your times.
  • Catalyst Shards from the Altar count at 25 WSS each, as if you sell them. Combined with one of your maps, a shard forces an event there, worth about as much at the estimated times.
  • Unique maps: the bosses of City of Ureh, Warlord of Blood, Na-Krul's Abyss, and Djinn's Domain drop extra uniques, or a treasure explosion, every kill. Rush them and leave: Unique maps: rush the bosses.
  • For the grail, put in your missing items under Your grail (it can take your Grail Planner list), and the Corrupted Ear you use: an ear works on every monster of a full clear, but on a run only on the map boss.
  • The calculator: the fields start at estimated times; type yours or drag the sliders. The line under each slider says where the runs come out ahead and where full clears do, every other time as it is; on the slider, the striped side is where full clears are ahead. Tick Skip on an event you'd rather not do: when it shows, you head for the boss.

docs.title: Unique maps: rush the bosses
docs.text: The bosses of four unique maps drop extra loot every kill, on top of their own: three of them random uniques, Djinn's Domain's two a treasure explosion of 60 items each. So when you get one of these maps, rush its bosses and leave: for the grail no other map comes close. Unique maps open only in Hell, one a game. Put your time for a rush in each row: from entering the map, teleporting to the bosses, and killing them (City of Ureh's: clearing Gregus Mazi's room and killing Zayl the Merciful; Warlord of Blood's: Cory the Imp and Onion the Accused too). The overhead above (making the game, town, and stash) comes on top; a unique map needs no rolling. The numbers count your missing items when Your grail has a list, and follow the magic find you picked.

docs.text: The average run and the average full clear over the maps you picked, events and their odds included.

docs.title: Ahead or behind: full clear against scout
docs.text: With your other times as they are. Above the line full clears come out ahead, below it the runs do. Point at the chart to read a spot; click or drag to try it.

docs.title: What stays fixed
docs.text:
• What drops doesn't change with the times, so a time only changes the hours. The drops come from a model of how the game spawns map events and rolls drops: each of the 29 T1–T3 maps played as often, runs on rare maps rolled to low density with no purple line, full clears on rare maps as a clearer keeps them (one corruption), magic find as set plus the map's own.
  • An event rolls on 34% of rare maps, each of the 9 kinds as often. You always find it: the Dark Wanderer, Treasure Fallen, and Corrupted Heroes bring all three, and a Bitter Depths map always has its portal.
  • The Bitter Depths: its 20 Lucion chests (3 items from the lesser chest loot and 2 from the better, opened at character level 95 with your magic find and the map's), Zoltun Kulle's own drop and his treasure explosion (60 items of a T3 map boss's loot, with no magic find), and the area's monsters with its 5 elite packs. Its 7 plain chests are left out (about 3% of the event).
  • A skipped event: when it shows (a three-spawn kind at its first spawn, the Spire at its obelisk), you head straight for the boss, since a map has one event and nothing is left to find. You lose its drops and save its time and the rest of the scout. Full clears still do every event: a full clear's time includes them.
  • "Worth doing below" compares a run doing the event with one skipping it, by what you compare, with your other times as they are; with your own maps it also counts the maps the event drops (Horazon's six, Treasure Fallen's) and the full clears they save.
  • Teleports per map come from scouting every layout of every map: the fastest route that fills every room an event can spawn in averages 110, a scout that brings every walkable spot on screen 276. A count between them mixes the two; one outside scales the nearer one.
  • A full clear's time includes the event when the map has one, and every full clear kills the boss. Trade value counts each unique and set item at its median asking price on the trade site (softcore ladder, 23 November) and the currency at its median ask (a stack's price split over its items): Worldstone Shards at 1, the runes from Fal to Cham, Splinters, essences, scarabs, unique maps, and perfect gems. Anything with fewer than 5 asks also counts its asks of late October and early November, leaving out any more than 5 times above or below the rest. Some currency counts at what it is worth over a season rather than at today's asks: Zod at 500 WSS, Catalyst Shards at 25 (sold, not used on your own maps), Corrupted Ears and sigils at 10, Pandemonium keys at 5, Hel, Io, Lum, Ko, and crafting infusions at 3, and El to Dol and the infused orbs at 1. Asks, not sales.
  • Gold counts Anya's Zakarum and Horadrim Orbs for rolling (2.7 rolls a map for the runs, 1.7 for full clears) and Gheed's offers; the runes, perfect gems, and jewels the rolls also eat are left out.

docs.title: How map events spawn
docs.text:
A map rolls its event once, when it is opened: 11% of non-magical, 17% of magic, and 34% of rare T1–T3 maps, one of nine kinds at equal odds. Nothing of it exists until it spawns. A room fills with monsters the first time you come near it: standing in one room fills it and the 8 rooms around it, about 24 tiles across, and a teleport fills the block around where you land. Each newly filled room may bring the event, more likely the more of the map's rooms are filled already; the event then stands in that room or one beside it, and its message shows.

EventWhen a newly filled room brings itSpawns The Bitter Depths, Horazon, the Shadow of Mendeln, Gheed, and the Altar of the CatalystNever before about 42% of the map's rooms are filled, then ever more often: usually about halfway through a scout1 The Dark Wanderer, the Treasure Fallen, and the Corrupted Heroes (a portal)The first once a quarter of the rooms are filled, the second past half, the third past three quarters, each 1 room in 43 The Spire of DarknessAfter 15 rooms, 1 room in 5. Once you use its obelisk, half the new rooms bring a group of shadows, until 6 keys or nine tenths of the rooms1

How many rooms count as the whole map is set per map, from the Lost Temple's few to the Halls of Torture's many, and the empty blocks at a map's edges count too. A spawn needs open ground near the room's center, about 2.4 tiles across, so the crowded corners of a map take none. Scouting every room is what makes the late kinds show: a scout that skips parts of the map can miss them.

docs.title: Map Experience
docs.text:
Season 14 · Maps · Experience

The filter puts two experience lines on identified maps: this page explains both, shows how your level and a map's size change the second one, and how the T4 dungeons compare.

Your character's level 89 The average non-magical map at level 89

Every map ranked The rolls The "at Level" line Your level Example T4 dungeons How it's worked out 11.48x Experience 21.14x at Level 89 Experience: +15% Monster Density: +47% 11.48x Experience

How much the map's rolls add to it. The same for every character. On uncorrupted maps only.

21.14x at Level 89

What the map is worth to you: experience for the distance you walk, against an average non-magical map, at your level.

Rule of thumb: pick which map to run by the "at Level" line. The "Experience" line tells you whether an uncorrupted map rolled well enough to corrupt.

The “Experience” tag: how good the rolls are

A full clear of this map with its rolls, against the same map with no rolls: 1.48x means the rolls add 48%. Which map it is doesn't matter here, only what its rolls add to it, and your level doesn't change it.

  • What counts: Monster Density (more monsters), Monster Rarity (more champion and unique packs), Experience, Area Level (higher level monsters, each worth more), Fortified (half as many monsters, each worth double), and "Map contains ..." monsters (one more kind of monster in the mix).
  • What doesn't: anything that makes monsters easier or harder to kill, and the loot rolls.
  • Where it shows: uncorrupted T1–T3 maps and T4 dungeons. It's there to tell you whether a map is worth corrupting; once it's corrupted, its rolls are settled and the "at Level" line says what it's worth to you. Unique maps don't show it: their rolls never change.
Its color

The color of the tag's number says how the rolls compare with other maps of the same tier (the word Experience is always gold): gold is good, red better, purple the best. Every tier is cut about the same way among uncorrupted rare maps: about 1 in 6 shows no line, about half are gold, 1 in 4 red, and 1 in 12 purple (a little fewer red and purple in T1, more in T3). Most magic maps, about 4 in 5, show no line. T4 dungeons always show it: about 6 in 10 gold, 3 in 10 red, and 1 in 10 purple. Can't tell the colors apart? The tag's number decides its color: compare it with this table.

Tier No line Gold Red Purple

T4 dungeons are cut among their uncorrupted rare dungeons, which the Horadric Cube makes from a T3 map and a Horadrim Scarab, with a preset +40–50% Experience on top of their rolls: more on dungeons below.

The “at Level” line: what the map is worth to you This map with its rolls: the experience of a full clear, for you, divided by the distance you walk to clear it The average non-magical T1–T3 map: the same, for you

1.0x is an average plain map. 1.1x is 10% more experience for the same distance walked. Below 1.0x, an average plain map would do better. T4 dungeons are compared with the average plain T3 map instead (T4 dungeons).

  • The map itself: how many monsters spawn, how many champion and unique packs, their level, and the bosses in its layout.
  • Its rolls: the same ones as in the Experience line.
  • The distance: every map has a clear path, the route that takes you close to 95% of the places its monsters spawn (most players clear 90–95% of a map), starting where you arrive and averaged over its layouts. A big, spread-out map takes longer to clear, so its experience counts for less.
  • Your level: monsters well below your level give less experience. More on that below.
  • Your own +% experience: the map's Experience roll adds to the bonus you already have; it doesn't multiply it. So it's worth less the more you have: with an Annihilus (+10%), a map's +15% gives you about 14% more, not 15%.
Its color

The color of the line's number says how far ahead of an average non-magical map this map is for you (the words "at Level" are always gold): gold, then red, then purple, the furthest ahead. On T1–T3 and unique maps the number alone decides it, so a 2.5x is purple at any level. T4 dungeons, compared with the T3 maps and far ahead of them, have cuts of their own, which rise from level 95. Can't tell the colors apart? Compare the number with this table.

Maps Gold Red Purple

Of rare T1–T3 maps, about 1 in 3 shows red or purple and 1 in 20 purple. Corrupted T2 and T3 maps, the ones most players run at high levels, are red or purple far more often: about two in three at level 94. Dungeons are made from T3 maps and can be corrupted like them, so their cuts give them about as much color as a T3 map at your level: an uncorrupted dungeon as often as an uncorrupted T3 map, a corrupted one as often as a corrupted T3 map (at level 94, about 1 in 4 uncorrupted rare dungeons shows red or purple, and two in three corrupted ones, 1 in 5 of them purple). A dungeon's line climbs from level 95, and its cuts climb with it: why.

At your level

Set your level in the bar at the top of the page: this section and the example's table follow it.

Maps to level 90

Experience from each monster at level 89

Map monsters are level 87 in T1, 88 in T2, 89 in T3, and 92 in T4 dungeons. Champions are 2 levels higher, uniques and their minions 3. A monster up to 5 levels below you gives full experience, and each level more takes 19% off, down to 5%. A monster above your level gives your level divided by its level.

Tier Normal monsters Champions+2 levels Uniques and minions+3 levels The average non-magical map of each tier

Your level counts for the average map too, so it only moves the line where a map's monsters are lower or higher than average. Up to about level 92 hardly anything moves. From there, T1 maps fall behind, T3 maps pull ahead, and an Area Level roll is worth more.

    Show as a table Example: the Sanatorium above

    An uncorrupted T1 map with +47% Monster Density and +15% Experience.

    1. Its rolls: a full clear gives 1.485x the experience of a non-magical Sanatorium. Cut to two decimals: 1.48x Experience, gold.
    2. The map: a non-magical Sanatorium has about as many monsters as the average map (its full clear: 1.01x), but its clear path is 1.32x the average's, one of the longest of the T1 maps. Per distance walked that's 0.77x.
    3. Together: 0.77 × 1.485 ≈ 1.143, shown as 1.14x at Level 89.

    The same map at other levels, with an Annihilus (+10% experience), and as if it had rolled +1 to Area Level as well:

    Your level This map With an Annihilus (+10%) With +1 Area Level T4 dungeons

    The Horadric Cube makes a dungeon from a T3 map and a Horadrim Scarab (the map can be non-magical, magic, or rare), or from three dungeons. Every dungeon comes out rare, with six random affixes of its own. On top of those, the recipe gives every dungeon the same five preset affixes, each rolled within its range:

    • +40–50% Experience, added to any Experience its random affixes roll
    • Monsters have 20–30% increased Velocity
    • Monsters have +80–100% Attack Rating and Chance to Pierce
    • Monsters' melee attacks deal splash damage
    • Monsters Cannot Be Frozen and have 10–20% increased Maximum Life

    Only the Experience counts in the two lines: the other four make its monsters faster, harder hitting, and longer to kill, not worth more. A dungeon's affixes can't be rerolled, but it can be corrupted like a map. A dungeon has two floors, and its monsters are level 92: champions 94, uniques and their minions 95.

    ⚠

    Dangerous and deadly. Every dungeon monster has several immunities and hits hard, and a dungeon can take upwards of 45 minutes to an hour or longer. The "at Level" line counts experience for the distance you walk, not for the time you spend, and a dungeon's monsters take far longer to kill than a map's: its number doesn't tell you what a dungeon gives you an hour.

    Why its line is so high

    Each dungeon at level 89

    Full clear: both floors, before the dungeon's rolls, against the average plain T3 map, before your level counts. Clear path: its length against the average T3 map's. Average rare and Corrupted: the "at Level" line an average rare dungeon shows you, as it comes from the Cube and with one corruption.

    Dungeon Full clear Clear path Average rare Corrupted From level 80 to 98

    Each dungeon's "at Level" line at every level: almost flat up to level 94, then climbing.

    Average rare Corrupted
      Show as a table Dungeons to level 90

      What it leaves out
      • How fast you kill: monster life, damage, resistances, immunities, and your build. It assumes the time a clear takes grows with the distance you walk.
      • Loot: Magic Find and the drop rolls.
      • Random map events.
      • Everything between maps: time in town, loading screens, opening maps.
      Good to know
      • The lines show on identified maps only: an unidentified map has no rolls yet. The "Experience" line shows on uncorrupted T1–T3 maps and T4 dungeons only.
      • The "at Level" line shows for characters of level 80–98. At level 99 there's no experience to gain, so there's no line.
      • The tag is cut to two decimals, so its number always matches its color: 1.649 shows as 1.64x. The "at Level" line is rounded to two decimals: 1.155 shows as 1.16x, and 0.999 as 1.00x. Its color follows the number shown, so 1.996 is a red 2.00x.
      • They are estimates, worked out from how maps are built and how monsters spawn, not counted in game.
      How it's worked out
      • Monsters. Every area of a map spawns monsters in its rooms. Monster Density adds spawns, up to a limit each area has. Champion and unique packs fall between the area's own minimum and maximum, and Monster Rarity raises both. Fortified halves the spawns and doubles each monster's experience. A "Map contains ..." monster joins the area's own monsters as one more kind, picked for about 1 spawn in 10 (1 in 7 to 1 in 20, depending on the area). The bosses and monsters placed in a map's layout count too.
      • Experience per monster. It follows the monster's level: the map's area level, plus any Area Level roll (each level is worth about 2.5% more around level 87), 2 more for champions and 3 more for uniques and their minions.
      • Your level. Each kind of monster gets the level penalty above: 81%, 62%, 43%, 24%, and then 5% for a monster 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10 or more levels below you. Then your own +% experience and the map's are added together and applied.
      • Clear path. Measured on the map's own layouts, starting where you arrive (the map start on the wiki's layout pictures: on T1–T3 maps, the waypoint): walk to the nearest place a monster can spawn that you haven't come within 7 tiles of yet, then put those stops in the shortest order found and walk them again, leaving out the hardest-to-reach places, until you've come within 7 tiles of 95% of them. Averaged over every layout of the map, and over walks begun at the start and a few steps from it. Horazon's Memory's lightning spires are left out (players walk past them).
      • The 1.0x. The average of the 29 T1–T3 maps with no rolls: their average experience for you over their average clear path. For T4 dungeons, the average of the T3 maps.
      • T4 dungeons. The average rare dungeon's rolls come from rolling many dungeons the way the game does, six random affixes plus the five preset ones: on average +107% Monster Density, +10% Monster Rarity, and +65% Experience. The corrupted one takes each of the ten ways a corruption can go, one in ten each, on top of those: on average +41% Monster Density, +17% Monster Rarity, and +2% Experience more, and +1 Area Level 1 time in 10. Dungeons to your next level count full clears of both floors, the average of the three dungeons.

docs.title: How to read them
docs.text:
A line's color says how much it matters; its number is the map's own.

Gray worth knowing Red dangerous Purple very dangerous Teal a bonus

The share beside each line is how many of the maps picked in the bar show it, out of maps rolled the way the game rolls them (every map of the tier as likely). Treacherous maps (made with a Corrupted Ear) and unique maps aren't counted. A line of the monsters a map holds counts the maps rolled with them and, for a map's own monsters, the tier's maps it names. Lines that also depend on the damage of a map's own monsters (+X% Fire Damage on maps whose monsters deal fire), Melee Splash, and Dual Extra Damage on corrupted maps have no share beside them; "not on these maps" is a line the maps picked never show.

docs.title: Your character
docs.text:
These lines depend on the character hovering the map, not only on the map. Put in yours (all as your character screen shows them) to see when each one shows for you.

Block on gear: your shield's Chance to Block plus any +% block on other gear. Weakest resistance over the cap: how far your lowest of fire, cold, and lightning is over its maximum (85% with a 75% cap is 10). The share on the right is how many of the maps in the bar show the line for you.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• In a map, your character already has that map's penalties, so a line that follows your character counts the map you stand in on top of the one you hover: it shows stronger, never weaker.
  • Hit chance lines (Player Defense, Attack Rating) are for a normal monster of the map's level with that level's usual attack rating.
  • Monster Defense follows your attack rating, which the line works out from your character with a usual bonus for your class's attack skills, so it isn't in the form above. Casters (more cast rate than attack speed) never see it.

docs.title: How it adds up
docs.text: A dashed step adds into a pool; a solid one multiplies. Numbers are for an average roll.

docs.title: The rules behind it
docs.text:
• +% damage adds up, then multiplies the physical part once. One pool holds the map's Enhanced Physical Damage, Fortified's 40, the elite bonus (Hell: champion 66, Berserker 198), Extra Strong (unique 99, its minions 49), and Might, Concentration, or Fanaticism.
  • Deadly strike multiplies the physical part by 1.5, after that pool. It never touches elemental damage.
  • Many monsters' attacks carry elemental damage of their own, on every hit or on a share of them, which grows with the monster's level and the players in the game as its physical damage does. Spectral Hit's element takes the place of the attack's own damage of that element.
  • Elemental damage of one kind is one roll. "Physical damage as extra", the attack's own, Fire, Cold, and Lightning Enchanted, Holy Fire and Holy Shock's added damage, and Spectral Hit all add to it; then the skill damage mods (Flaming, Hibernal, Static, Toxic, and Fortified's) raise it. +% damage and deadly strike don't.
  • "Physical damage as extra" is a share of the monster's base attack, before the +% pool and deadly strike. The poison version's number is per frame: over its 5 seconds it deals 125/256 of what it says (163% shown is about 80%).
  • Enchanted uniques add 66–100% of their level's damage figure to their attacks in that element; their minions 33–50%.
  • Spectral Hit adds 66–100% of the unique's level damage figure to each attack in one random element: fire, lightning, magic, cold, or poison (1 attack in 5 each). Its poison is a per-frame figure too: alone it deals 40/256 of it over 1.6 seconds. On a map that adds poison, a hit with both lasts 290 frames instead of 125, so all of its poison deals 290/256 of its figure.
  • Aura Enchanted gives a unique one of eight monster auras (Conviction, Fanaticism, Holy Shock, Holy Freeze, Holy Fire, Might, Concentration, and Vigor) at its level / 7, at most 13: a unique is 3 levels above the area, so that's level 12 in T1 maps and 13 in T2 and up (or with +1 area level). Holy Fire, Holy Freeze, and Holy Shock add their damage to the unique's own attacks; Vigor changes no hit numbers here.
  • Cursed casts Amplify Damage on 3 of a unique's hits in 4, at its level / 5 + 1: level 19 in T1–T3 maps, 20 in T4 dungeons.
  • Some bosses have an aura of their own, always on, and its damage joins their attacks: Son of Rakkis's Holy Shock (level 15) and Shattered Soul's Holy Freeze (level 10).
  • The 5% double comes last and doubles everything in the hit. With deadly strike too, the physical part is 3x. It's each monster's own chance (5% for nearly all; T4 dungeons' Blood Bringers, the Outer Void's Void Knights, and the bosses Gregus Mazi, Overlord Aerlynn, and Warlord of Blood have none), and it doubles spells and missiles as well as melee hits.
  • A boss's spells deal their own damage, at their skill level (7 higher in Hell than in Normal): the monster's level and the players in the game don't change it. The map's +% fire, cold, lightning, and poison skill damage and Fortified's raise its elemental part, as they do the attack's; a few missiles carry damage of their own that they don't raise. The +% damage pool, deadly strike, "physical damage as extra", and the attack's own elemental damage only reach the spells that strike with a share of the boss's attack (that share of each).
  • Fire on the ground (a fire wall, the burning ground a meteor or a blaze leaves) hits again and again while you stand in it, up to 25 times a second, and takes its share of your flat damage reduction each time: the page shows a second standing in it.
  • Fortified adds 40 to the +% damage pool, though the orb's text says +20%.
  • Curses and Conviction lower your totals, the same way the map's -resist does. Your physical damage reduction counts up to 50% against a hit and your resistances up to your maximum (at most 90%), so anything above that soaks them first. Amplify Damage and Decrepify lower physical damage reduction; Lower Resist lowers fire, cold, lightning, and poison; Conviction fire, cold, and lightning.
  • Crushing blow ignores the hit's damage: it takes a tenth of your current life, less your whole physical damage reduction (curses included, not capped at 50%). At 100% or more it does nothing.
  • Flat damage reduction comes off physical damage before the percentage; magic damage reduction off fire, cold, lightning, and magic. Poison ignores both.
  • Each player after the first adds 6.25% to monsters' base attack damage (and 70% to their life).
  • Not counted here: how often you're hit (attack rating, defense, block, and attack speed), the pulse damage of the auras a monster gets from a unique mod or a monster near it (Holy Fire, Holy Shock, and Holy Freeze), open wounds, absorb, poison length reduction, how many of a spell's bolts or shards reach you, and the spells and missiles of monsters other than bosses.

Season 14 · Weapons · Sockets

Does a jewel beat an Ohm rune in your weapon? Pick the weapon and what is already on it: the page works out, to the point, how much minimum and maximum damage a jewel needs to match Ohm’s enhanced damage, and how the jewels that can drop compare.

Average hit

With Ohm With your jewel

Each bar runs from the minimum to the maximum damage; the mark on it is the average hit.

docs.title: What a jewel needs to match Ohm
Jewels that can roll
docs.text:
Each jewel has one affix of each kind at most: enhanced damage, minimum or maximum damage as a prefix, and minimum or maximum damage as a suffix. A magic jewel has one prefix and one suffix; a rare jewel four affixes, three of a side at most. Each line is its affixes of the highest tiers, against Ohm in this weapon at their lowest and their top rolls, the best first.

Worse than OhmBetter than OhmOhmEach bar runs from the lowest to the top rolls.

docs.title: How it’s worked out
docs.text:
• Enhanced damage on the weapon raises only its base damage. The weapon’s own enhanced damage, a superior base’s, and every rune and jewel in its sockets add up, and the weapon’s damage is its base damage plus that percentage of it, rounded down. Its minimum and maximum damage (affixes, sockets) are added after, so enhanced damage never raises them.
  • An ethereal weapon has 5/4 of its base’s damage, rounded down, before anything else.
  • Ohm against a jewel: Ohm adds 45% of the base damage, a jewel its own enhanced damage of it plus its flat damage. A jewel needs the flat damage that makes up the difference, which the page works out with the rounding of the weapon you entered: one point either way decides it more often than not.
  • Everything else multiplies both alike. Strength or Dexterity, skills, auras, and enhanced damage on other gear raise the weapon’s damage by the same percentage with Ohm or with the jewel, and flat damage from other gear (rings, charms) is the same either way, so the difference in the weapon’s damage decides. The page compares the weapon’s damage; your whole attack differs by a little less when other gear adds flat damage.
  • A hit rolls any damage from its minimum to its maximum alike, so the average hit is halfway between. When a jewel’s minimum damage lifts the minimum to the maximum or above, the maximum becomes the minimum + 1.
  • Sockets go up to the most the base can have (at item level 41 or higher).

Inspired by HarryPe’s Physical damage calculator (its “Ohm vs jewel in Weapons” sheet).

Each setup from a standing start, its buffs just cast, at the game’s own speed and scale. The legs move as fast as the game moves them. A buff that runs out on the way (Blaze, Joust) stops counting there.

RunningWalking Distance 10 yards20 yards30 yards50 yards100 yards Speed As in gameHalf speedQuarter speed Run the race Loading the pictures…

docs.text: Add a setup Clear setups Reset to the defaults Copy a link to this setup

docs.title: Speed and FRW on gear
docs.text: Each line is a setup’s running speed (its whirlwinding speed when it has Whirlwind) as its FRW on gear goes from 0 to 300%, its skills as they are; the dot, with the setup’s letter, is where it is now. The dashed gray line is a character running with no movement skills.

docs.title: How it’s worked out
docs.text:
• FRW on gear (with Vigor’s +1% per base point: the Paladin has it whichever aura is on) adds up, then counts as 150 × FRW / (150 + FRW), rounded down: 30% counts 25, 60% counts 42, 100% counts 60, 300% counts 100.
  • Movement from skills (Increased Speed, Frenzy, Burst of Speed, Vigor’s aura, Blaze, Evade, Feral Rage, Hunger, Joust) and from a Stamina shrine (+35%) counts in full. Frenzy’s grows with its stacks (a fifth of it per stack, full at 5); Feral Rage’s is worked out from its charges, as the game does. Feral Rage is the werewolf’s and Hunger the werebear’s, so a Druid has one of them at a time.
  • Blaze gives +25% movement at level 1 and 1% more a level, up to 60%, while it lasts: 3 seconds at level 1 and 0.2 more a level, up to 10. Any class can have it from an item (Infernostride casts level 16 when you’re struck: +40% for 6 seconds). It’s one effect, so a Sorceress’s own Blaze and an item’s don’t add up: the page counts one at a time. While it lasts it leaves fire behind you as you move, and each flame burns for 2.4 seconds.
  • Charge sets its own speed when it starts: the run speed with Charge’s +150% added to the movement % from skills, shrines, and slows (at least 50%, so Decrepify or a chill slows a charge too). FRW and running’s +50% don’t count, so it’s 23.44 yards a second with nothing else. In the race the Paladin charges the whole way (the strike at the end left out; when a buff runs out it charges again). Its legs play a frame of the run each game frame whatever the speed, and the two fainter copies behind it stand for Charge’s trails.
  • Whirlwind moves you at walking speed with every movement % that counts while walking (FRW on gear as above, your skills, a shrine, slows) plus Whirlwind’s own: the “Velocity” its description shows, +2% for each level after the first, up to +65% from level 34. Running’s +50% doesn’t count, so FRW and your other bonuses raise your whirlwinding speed as they raise your walking speed. With 40% FRW and Whirlwind 20 (+38%) and nothing else, that’s 10.56 yards a second whirlwinding against 11.31 running. In the race the Barbarian whirls the whole way, in the attack pose Whirlwind holds him in, with its own effect around him.
  • Speed: walking is 6 points of speed, running 9 (walking + 50%), and every 1% of movement adds 0.06 of a point. The game moves you a sixteenth of a map square per point every frame, 25 frames a second; in the yards the skill descriptions use (a map square is two thirds of a yard), a point is 25/24 of a yard a second: walking 6.25, running 9.375, and every 1% adds 0.0625. Calculators that read the points as yards a second show about 4% less. The speed never goes below a quarter of walking.
  • The race uses the game’s own pictures, facing east (screen right), where a yard is 34 of the game’s pixels across. The animation keeps pace with the speed: running plays 101/256 of a frame per game frame and walking 213/256 (the werewolf 104 and 128, the werebear 120 and 168), times the same speed % that moves you, so a faster character also moves its legs faster. Each setup starts with its buffs just cast, and a buff that runs out on the way stops counting there: Joust’s lasts 2 seconds and Blaze’s 3 to 10, the others longer than any race here.
  • Slows take off the same movement % your skills add to, in full. Cold damage chills you for −50% while it lasts. A monster’s Decrepify, Holy Freeze, or Slow Movement takes what its skill level gives, and a monster’s skills are 3 levels higher in Nightmare and 7 in Hell. Duriel’s Holy Freeze is the exception: −42% in Normal and Nightmare and −44% in Hell. Map bosses, map events, and ubers are in Hell. An aura-enchanted unique monster has one of 8 auras, Holy Freeze among them, at its own level divided by 7 (at most 13): from −30% at monster level 1 to 13 up to −51% at level 91 and above, in every difficulty. In the race, chill and Holy Freeze turn the runner blue and Decrepify and Slow Movement show their effects, as the game draws them. Slows add up with each other and with your buffs: chilled with Frenzy’s +58%, you keep +8%. Armor and shields don’t slow you.
  • Not shown: Blade Dance’s own movement, Teleport, and what stops you for a moment (spider webs, a map boss’s stun).

Inspired by HarryPe’s Physical damage calculator (its “FRW Calculator” sheet).

Season 14 · Maps · Runes

How often each rune drops, playing solo: per kill and per map in T1–T3 maps, with a Corrupted Ear and map events, in T4 dungeons, from every boss and farm spot, and in every Hell area.

Rune Count This runeAnd higher Map Corrupted Ear NoneAn ear Map events Left outCounted Reset to the defaultsCopy a link to this setup

PlaceWhere ChanceMonster level

Area Act Monster level A monster A champion A unique and its minions How it's worked out
  • One kill, one drop. A monster drops from its own item pool, which grows with its level: the higher the level, the more of it can be high runes. From about level 85, every Hell monster can drop every rune.
  • Uniques drop more. A unique monster picks from its pool more than once, so it is worth about two normal monsters, and each of its minions one. A champion drops as a normal monster does.
  • A map is a full clear of the tier's average map, its boss included: about 1,250 kills a non-magical map and 2,300 to 2,600 a rare one, which has more monsters and more packs.
  • Rare maps are corrupted. A rare map here is the average one with a corruption, as most are run: +91%, +104%, or +117% monster density and +14%, +18%, or +23% monster rarity on T1, T2, or T3. An uncorrupted rare map has fewer monsters and packs, so it finds runes less often per map (a kill's chance hardly changes). A non-magical map has no rolls.
  • A Corrupted Ear rolls each monster's drop a second time some of the time and adds packs, which is why it finds runes faster. The extra gear an ear drops is no rune.
  • Map events counted are the Bitter Depths (its monsters, Zoltun Kulle, his treasure explosion, and its Lucion chests) and the Hell Bovines (the Bovine maps and the Dark Wanderer's Cow King), as often as maps have them. Other events are left out. Running maps for their events and bosses instead of clearing them: Map Event and Boss Rushing.
  • T4 dungeons: the average rare dungeon with a corruption (+148% monster density, +27% rarity). Every monster drops twice, and both bosses set off a treasure explosion.
  • Bosses and farm spots drop at most six items a kill, as in game. A superunique's minions are counted with it.
  • Magic find does nothing for runes.
  • Solo. In a party the chance a monster drops nothing gets smaller: about 10% more runes with 3 or more players.
  • "Half find one by" and "9 in 10 by": how many maps (or kills) it takes until half of the players, or 9 in 10, have found at least one. On average, one comes every "A map" maps.

docs.title: Shadow of Mendeln
docs.text:
Season 14 · Maps · Map events

Shadow of Mendeln is a map event that summons 45 waves of undead in 72 seconds: this page shows what they are worth to you, and the four choices that make them worth more.

Your level 95 Map T1 T2 T3 The map has +1 area level Fortified Players in your party 1 Reset to the defaultsCopy a link to this setup of level experience full clears of a non-magical map full clears of a corrupted rare map

Your +% experience % An Annihilus gives 5–10%. Add the map's Experience roll if it has one. How it's worked out
  • The waves. Waves 1–20 bring 0–7 normal monsters each; waves 21–35 0–5 normal monsters and 0–2 champions; waves 36–45 0–3 normal monsters, 0–1 champion, and 0–2 uniques, each unique with 3–6 minions. On average that is . Four in five are Hungry Dead, Defiled Warriors, Horrors, or Horror Archers, one in five a Horror Mage; all give the same experience.
  • Each monster's experience. The same for every wave monster of a map: , for one player. Champions give 3 times as much and are 2 levels higher; 1 in 5 is a berserker, 5 times as much and 3 levels higher. Uniques give 5 times as much and are 3 levels higher. A unique's minions give the plain experience, at the map's level.
  • Players and your party. Each player in the game after the first adds 50% when the monster spawns. A kill is shared by the party members within about 53 yards: together they get 1 + 0.35 for each member after the first, split between them by level (this page takes everyone at your level).
  • Your level. A monster up to 5 levels below you gives its full experience, then 81%, 62%, 43%, and 24% at 6, 7, 8, and 9 levels below, and 5% from 10 levels below. A monster above your level gives your level divided by its level. From level 70 a character gets only part of every kill's experience, less the higher it is: . Then your +% experience (your own and the map's add up).
  • Fortified: every kill counts twice.
  • Full clears. The tier's average map from the model the Map Experience page explains: every monster a full clear of each map spawns, and its level. Non-magical, or the average corrupted rare map (T1 / T2 / T3: ). The same setup counts for both: a Fortified or +1 area level map's own clear is Fortified or +1 too.
  • Left out: how long the kills take (the waves have the map's life, +70% for each player after the first and twice as much on a Fortified map), Mendeln's curses, and a monster that finds no room near him to spawn.

docs.title: Four choices make it bigger
docs.text:
Fortified

Every kill counts twice, the event's too. A Fortified map has half as many monsters of its own, each worth twice as much, so its clear gives about what the same map gives without it. The event isn't halved: on a Fortified map it is worth twice as much.

A party

Each player in the game after the first adds 50% to every monster's experience, and your party shares every kill near it. With 8 players each of you gets times what one player alone would. It makes no difference who gets the kills.

A higher tier

The waves are as high as the map's area level: 87 in T1, 88 in T2, and 89 in T3. Up to level 92 that changes almost nothing. From there your level takes experience off monsters 6 or more levels below you: a T1 map's from level 93, a T2 map's from 94, a T3 map's from 95. The higher the map, the less it loses.

+1 area level

One of a map corruption's outcomes, 9% of them. A T1 map with it gives what a T2 map does, a T2 map what a T3 map does, and a T3 map with it (area level 90) is the most there is. Fortify a corrupted map: the Horadric Cube takes it.

docs.title: Every map, at level
docs.text:
Map Neither +1 area level Fortified Fortified,+1 area level

A T1 map with +1 area level gives exactly what a T2 map without it does, and a T2 map with +1 what a T3 map does: the waves are as high as the map's area level, whichever tier it is.

docs.title: Your level decides how much the map counts
docs.text:
Each map's event against a T1 map's at the same level. Up to level 92 every map gives about the same. From 93 your level starts to take experience off monsters 6 or more levels below you, and the higher area levels pull ahead: at 98 a T3 map with +1 area level gives times a T1 map. Players, Fortified, and your +% experience don't change these lines: they multiply every map alike.
